NHI: Irish Medical Exodus: South African Doctors seek greener pastures in Ireland

By: Nickolaus Bauer | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South Africa’s NHI dream risks collapse as South African doctors leave for better opportunities abroad, fuelling a critical healthcare brain drain

Unique Selling Point:
An exclusive viewpoint of South African doctors abroad that have left South Africa due to a lack of opportunities and ability to specialise in a field of their choice. Exposing the pitfalls of implementing a universal healthcare system without the requisite medical personnel which are choosing to leave the country.

Summary:
The government's National Health Insurance (NHI) plan that envisions South Africa as a healthcare hub characterised by modern medical infrastructure supporting universal access. Bu that will remain a pipe dream if the country fails to retain its highly skilled and experienced medical Doctors which are seeking opportunities abroad.
Dr. Lindsay Kaberry and Dr Ememabasi Edem, South African doctors now practicing in Mayo and Tipperary in Ireland represent just two of thousands of medical professionals who have left South Africans. This personal story anchors an exploration of the healthcare brain drain from South Africa, examining the causes and consequences of this exodus. As well as how a national health insurance system works elsewhere and its challenges.

Further information:
*INTRO START*

VO: Government wants you to believe National Health Insurance will be the answer to ALL South Africa’s medical problems.

NHI AD
Maybe the NHI will be the solution. I don't know. NHI, seems a bit communist

VO: But state funding for existing medical care is already floundering

AARON Motsoaledi
Very brutal budget cuts that affect not only our capacity to hire doctors, but to perform quite a large number of functions.

VO: And doctor’s are considering their options overseas

Graham Cosgrave
It certainly is a feeding frenzy, particularly for family medicine doctors from South Africa.

Dr Ememabasi Edem
We've done our time. We're grateful for the experience that we've had in South Africa.
But I don't think that anyone should be shackled

VO: Many worried about the implications of NHI

Neville Staples
Visa applications to the immigration office behind us here for the next batch of South African doctors

Dr Lindsay Kaberry
Even though it's sad to leave. This was the best move for myself and my family.

*INTRO END*

OPENING PTC
Hundreds of South African doctors are leaving for Ireland annually, with various push and pull factors being behind their move. The opportunity to specialise in a medical field of their choice, the chance to escape crime or political instability back home. Their skills and experience gained in South Africa are welcomed with open arms in hospitals like this, enriching the quality of care in the Emerald Isle and throwing into question our own plans to implement national healthcare insurance back home.

VO: Despite disagreements within the Government of National Unity…

VO: Several legal challenges… (MAIL & GUARDIAN FOOTAGE USED UNDER AGREEMENT)


VO: And question marks over funding… (MAIL & GUARDIAN FOOTAGE USED UNDER AGREEMENT)


VO: Government is determined National Health Insurance WILL proceed.

VO: And has already spent thirty million rand promoting the system.

NHI ADVERT
“Honey! You know what keeps me up at night, hey? Its the rising costs of medical aid with less cover…”“NHI is our answer for quality healthcare for all of us. Even you my babe…” (DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH FOOTAGE USED UNDER THE PREMISE OF FAIR USAGE)
VO: But how is this going to work?
VO: Government can’t meet current public health demands or even employ all the doctors it needs.
VO: Many South Africans view the public healthcare system as a deathtrap
VO: 1800 newly qualified doctors are also unemployed. And doctors are being told to seek work overseas if they want to …

BYTE: AARON MOTSOALEDI, HEALTH MINISTER
You are a free person. You are a free fully fledged doctor. You can go anywhere. If the state advertises a post, you can apply. If the post is in a private sector, you can apply. If you want to open your own private practice, you can and do so. If you want to go and work elsewhere, you can do anything. (NEWZROOM AFRIKA FOOTAGE USED UNDER THE PREMISE OF FAIR USAGE)

VO: Joburger Dr Lindsay Kaberry works at Mayo University Hospital in the West of Ireland as an emergency department consultant.
VO: She studied at Wits University, did her internship at Sebokeng hospital and community service in Parys. Before working in the public and private for 5 years.

BYTE:DR LINDSAY KABERRY, South African doctor at Mayo University Hospital

“There’s a lot of South African doctors already in Ireland. Mostly in Dublin, Cork and Limerick. So I came out to the West - more rural.”

QUESTION: NICKOLAUS BAUER
Did the introduction of NHI in South Africa figure in your decision to come to Ireland?
BYTE:DR LINDSAY KABERRY, South African doctor at Mayo University Hospital
“I was very worried about the NHI, mainly because I was a private GP, and we didn't know how we were going to get paid. So the thing is. Where is the money coming from?”

VO: NHI has been on the government's agenda for 15 years. And will create a centralized national insurance fund for universal healthcare, funded by all South Africans - by pooling state and private resources.
VO: While promising equitable access, it would effectively abolish the current private medical care system.

BYTE:DR LINDSAY KABERRY, South African doctor at Mayo University Hospital
It's a pipe dream. They're trying to model it as a first world country where we don't have the resources for it. Where the majority of the patients are using the public sector, So realistically, I don't see it working.

VO: Alongside the typical reasons for emigration, for Dr Kaberry and South African physicians like her, NHI is the final straw. And for Irish medical recruiters business is booming.

VO: Match Medics recruited two hundred South African doctors last year alone. With their planned roadshow to South Africa at the end of March expected to attract over three thousand Doctors considering a move.

BYTE: GRAHAM COSGRAVE, Match Medics
I've been a medical recruiter for well over a decade now, personally, and I haven't seen the demand to move to Ireland as high as it is today. Some South Africans might come here and say it as a year or two years, just a bit of an adventure. The majority are moving their entire lives here.

QUESTION: Nickolaus Bauer
From what you're telling me, it seems like there's a feeding frenzy for South African doctors in Ireland?

BYTE:GRAHAM COSGRAVE
I can simply pick up the phone. If I have a strong South African doctor, I'll have ten clinical leads who I know I can call to say, this is the profile that I have, and they won't even have to be a publicly advertised job there for them to consider. They will bite our hands off to speak with them.

VO: With the Irish health sector is hoovering up South African doctors…
VO: Gqeberha native Neville Staples, started his own medical recruitment agency based on the sheer demand he witnessed when immigrating here 5 years ago.

BYTE:NEVILLE STAPLES, Rainbow Medical Recruitment
That's a big drain from South Africa, if you consider all the doctors that go through an MBCHB in South Africa.
Their two years internship, their postcom, serve years, and then they relocate. South Africa’s losing those brains. I come from the medical establishment back in South Africa. I've worked in it for Decades. It's going to kill it. It's a recipe for disaster. You cannot lose that amount of doctors and HPS, allied healthcare professionals on an annual basis, and not expect it to have a severe knock on effect.

VO: The Irish government wont say exactly how many South African doctors are practicing in the country… But it’s not just experienced Doctors.

VO: Dr Ememabasi Edem is a freshly minted medic that decided to make a move to Tipperary in the centre of Ireland directly after his year of community service at Tembisa hospital last year.

BYTE:DR EMEMABASI EDEM, South African doctor in Ireland
“It might be the opinion of some people that I should feel bad about leaving, but, I mean, I have my own dreams. I have my own ambitions, my own goals. And I don't think that working in health should preclude me from going for them.”

QUESTION: NICKOLAUS BAUER
And how would you compare the case loads with South Africa?

BYTE:DR EMEMABASI EDEM, South African doctor in Ireland
“We still see a lot of patients, but I think that. It's a lot better resourced. We get scans a lot faster. We never run out of equipment. And our health it sounds facetious to say, but our healthcare professionals are paid on time.”

BYTE:DR LINDSAY KABERRY, South African doctor at Mayo University Hospital
“The thing is, here, the equipment's working, so your beds are working, so if you put the patient on the bed, you're not worried that the rails aren't working. Whereas in South Africa, your beds aren't working, your chairs aren't working, you have patients sleeping on the floor. I've never seen it like that here.”

VO: Ireland is a wealthy country with a tiny population. And while it may seem a lot greener on this side for South African doctors…
That's not necessarily the case for patients in their public sector.

LINK PTC:
No national healthcare system is perfect, regardless of any guarantee of access to treatment. The usual challenges remain never, ending queues. Long waiting lists for critical procedures and hidden costs after operations are common issues, even Irish citizens face too. With decades, old national healthcare coverage.

VO: Like South Africa, Ireland has a mixed public-private healthcare system.

VO: Offering high-quality care in public hospitals, including emergency, maternity, and mental health services.

VO: But, with over 900,000 patients—nearly 20% of the population —on public waiting lists for specialized care, many face delays of months or even years for treatment.

VO: The handful we spoke to, hesitant to go on the record about their frustrations. For fear of being knocked further down the waiting list.

BYTE: GRAHAM COSGRAVE, Match Medics
“There's frustrations with the system, both as a patient, done as a doctor, 100 %. You know, we can't shy away from that. No system is perfect. There's pain points in the Irish system 100 %.”

As Dr Kaberry starts her new life in Ireland… She’ll help tackle that backlog. Using the critical skills she painstakingly learned in South Africa to do so.


INTERACTION
NICKOLAUS BAUER
How have you gotten used to this weather? This is nothing like South Africa.
DR LINDSAY KABERRY
It's not. But you get, you're surprising. You got really used to it.

NICKOLAUS BAUER
Do you feel guilty about leaving? I mean: South Africa trained you, you’re a doctor because of South Africa’s medical institutions.
DR LINDSAY KABERRY
I feel guilty leaving my patients behind. But I don’t feel guilty leaving South Africa. South Africa’s training was unparalleled. I would never take that away from them. You studied so hard, you worked so hard. And now I have to uproot my life to do what I wanted to do in the first place. I resent South Africa in a way that they didn’t offer the opportunities I wanted.

The Health Department didn’t respond to our questions about exactly how many doctors have left South Africa - neither did it address concerns about how this drain will impact the NHI scheme back home.

Because with doctor numbers dwindling… How can the system be a success?

QUESTION: NICKOLAUS BAUER
Is the implementation of national health insurance in South Africa even realistic at this point?

BYTE: NEVILLE STAPLES, Rainbow Medical Recruitment
Absolutely not. How are we going to service those patients? We have that issue anyway, doctors, there just aren't enough to serve as patients yet the Government isn't hiring enough of these doctors to fill that gap to fill that void. So if they can't get that right, I doubt whether they're going to get an NHI project right.

Press Release:


The Doctor’s Exodus

The government's National Health Insurance (NHI) plan envisions South Africa as a healthcare hub characterised by modern medical infrastructure supporting universal access. But that will remain a pipe dream if the country fails to retain its highly skilled and experienced medical Doctors who are seeking opportunities abroad. South Africa’s NHI dream risks collapse as more South African doctors leave for better opportunities abroad, fuelling a possible critical healthcare brain drain. In Ireland, scores of South African doctors are settling into their new life, after years spent training in their home country. Carte Blanche examines some of the causes and consequences of this exodus and asks: “Can the South Africa’s public healthcare system withstand the pressure of losing so many doctors?”

Producer & Presenter: Nickolaus Bauer

VO: But, with over 900,000 patients—nearly 20% of the population —on public waiting lists for specialized care, many face delays of months or even years for treatment. VO: The handful we spoke to, hesitant to go on the record about their frustrations. For fear of being knocked further down the waiting list. Using the critical skills she painstakingly learned in South Africa to do so. INTERACTION NICKOLAUS BAUER How have you gotten used to this weather? This is nothing like South Africa. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): South Africa’s NHI dream risks collapse as South African doctors leave for better opportunities abroad, fuelling a critical healthcare brain drain
metadata.Unique Selling Point: An exclusive viewpoint of South African doctors abroad that have left South Africa due to a lack of opportunities and ability to specialise in a field of their choice. Exposing the pitfalls of implementing a universal healthcare system without the requisite medical personnel which are choosing to leave the country.

Bu that will remain a pipe dream if the country fails to retain its highly skilled and experienced medical Doctors which are seeking opportunities abroad. Dr. Lindsay Kaberry and Dr Ememabasi Edem, South African doctors now practicing in Mayo and Tipperary in Ireland represent just two of thousands of medical professionals who have left South Africans. This personal story anchors an exploration of the healthcare brain drain from South Africa, examining the causes and consequences of this exodus. As well as how a national health insurance system works elsewhere and its challenges.

QUESTION: Nickolaus Bauer From what you're telling me, it seems like there's a feeding frenzy for South African doctors in Ireland? BYTE:GRAHAM COSGRAVE I can simply pick up the phone. If I have a strong South African doctor, I'll have ten clinical leads who I know I can call to say, this is the profile that I have, and they won't even have to be a publicly advertised job there for them to consider. They will bite our hands off to speak with them. VO: With the Irish health sector is hoovering up South African doctors… VO: Gqeberha native Neville Staples, started his own medical recruitment agency based on the sheer demand he witnessed when immigrating here 5 years ago. BYTE:NEVILLE STAPLES, Rainbow Medical Recruitment That's a big drain from South Africa, if you consider all the doctors that go through an MBCHB in South Africa. Their two years internship, their postcom, serve years, and then they relocate. South Africa’s losing those brains. I come from the medical establishment back in South Africa. I've worked in it for Decades. It's going to kill it. It's a recipe for disaster. You cannot lose that amount of doctors and HPS, allied healthcare professionals on an annual basis, and not expect it to have a severe knock on effect. VO: The Irish government wont say exactly how many South African doctors are practicing in the country… But it’s not just experienced Doctors. VO: Dr Ememabasi Edem is a freshly minted medic that decided to make a move to Tipperary in the centre of Ireland directly after his year of community service at Tembisa hospital last year. BYTE:DR EMEMABASI EDEM, South African doctor in Ireland “It might be the opinion of some people that I should feel bad about leaving, but, I mean, I have my own dreams. I have my own ambitions, my own goals. And I don't think that working in health should preclude me from going for them.” QUESTION: NICKOLAUS BAUER And how would you compare the case loads with South Africa? BYTE:DR EMEMABASI EDEM, South African doctor in Ireland “We still see a lot of patients, but I think that. It's a lot better resourced. We get scans a lot faster. We never run out of equipment. And our health it sounds facetious to say, but our healthcare professionals are paid on time.” BYTE:DR LINDSAY KABERRY, South African doctor at Mayo University Hospital “The thing is, here, the equipment's working, so your beds are working, so if you put the patient on the bed, you're not worried that the rails aren't working. Whereas in South Africa, your beds aren't working, your chairs aren't working, you have patients sleeping on the floor. I've never seen it like that here.” VO: Ireland is a wealthy country with a tiny population. And while it may seem a lot greener on this side for South African doctors… That's not necessarily the case for patients in their public sector. LINK PTC: No national healthcare system is perfect, regardless of any guarantee of access to treatment. The usual challenges remain never, ending queues. Long waiting lists for critical procedures and hidden costs after operations are common issues, even Irish citizens face too. With decades, old national healthcare coverage. VO: Like South Africa, Ireland has a mixed public-private healthcare system. VO: Offering high-quality care in public hospitals, including emergency, maternity, and mental health services. VO: But, with over 900,000 patients—nearly 20% of the population —on public waiting lists for specialized care, many face delays of months or even years for treatment. VO: The handful we spoke to, hesitant to go on the record about their frustrations. For fear of being knocked further down the waiting list. BYTE: GRAHAM COSGRAVE, Match Medics “There's frustrations with the system, both as a patient, done as a doctor, 100 %. You know, we can't shy away from that. No system is perfect. There's pain points in the Irish system 100 %.” As Dr Kaberry starts her new life in Ireland… She’ll help tackle that backlog. Using the critical skills she painstakingly learned in South Africa to do so. INTERACTION NICKOLAUS BAUER How have you gotten used to this weather? This is nothing like South Africa. DR LINDSAY KABERRY It's not. But you get, you're surprising. You got really used to it. NICKOLAUS BAUER Do you feel guilty about leaving? I mean: South Africa trained you, you’re a doctor because of South Africa’s medical institutions. DR LINDSAY KABERRY I feel guilty leaving my patients behind. But I don’t feel guilty leaving South Africa. South Africa’s training was unparalleled. I would never take that away from them. You studied so hard, you worked so hard. And now I have to uproot my life to do what I wanted to do in the first place. I resent South Africa in a way that they didn’t offer the opportunities I wanted. The Health Department didn’t respond to our questions about exactly how many doctors have left South Africa - neither did it address concerns about how this drain will impact the NHI scheme back home. Because with doctor numbers dwindling… How can the system be a success? QUESTION: NICKOLAUS BAUER Is the implementation of national health insurance in South Africa even realistic at this point? BYTE: NEVILLE STAPLES, Rainbow Medical Recruitment Absolutely not. How are we going to service those patients? We have that issue anyway, doctors, there just aren't enough to serve as patients yet the Government isn't hiring enough of these doctors to fill that gap to fill that void. So if they can't get that right, I doubt whether they're going to get an NHI project right.
